To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) natural resources have a negative and statistically significant effect on civil war onset, but no effect on the presence of civil wars, (2) natural resources have no statistically significant effects on the presence of ethnic civil wars, and (3) the size of the effect of natural resources on the presence of all types of civil war varies depending on the type of resource.
natural resources are not a significant factor in the onset of civil war, but they are a significant factor in civil war presence.

(1) life-preserving resources are associated with a lower risk of civil war; (2) income-generating resources are associated with an elevated risk of civil war, and (3) the effect of resources on civil war is due primarily to their life-preserv- ing and income-generating properties, and not their scarcity/abundance per se.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of resources as an explanatory variable of civil wars, not as a dependent one, and the effect may vary by the resource and by whether we examine civil wars onset versus presence.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the life-preserving and/or income-generating attributes of a resource matter, but the scarcity or abundance of the resource does not.
natural resources are not the main cause for civil wars but can play a role, and that the effect is not necessarily negative.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the role of natural resource abundance in civil war should be reconsidered.
we need to consider comprehensive and interrelated sets of natural resources to understand their role in civil war.
we need to consider a broad set of life-preserving/income-generating resources, and the interaction among them, to understand how natural resources affect civil wars.
